title: No caste, no charms
hookLine: the code rejects caste, untouchability, charms, idols and lucky days

lines: A CHARM BY THE DOOR, A STAR CHART.
cards: A charm hung by the door to keep bad luck out. A wedding moved to another month because the stars were wrong. A family that won't let a certain neighbor drink from their cups.

Scenes like these turn up in many times and places, the Gurus' Punjab among them. People reach for them because life is uncertain and a charm feels like control, or because a ranking of people feels like order.
The Sikh code takes them up, one after another, and sets them down.

teach.b: Back in year three, this path looked at caste and how the Gurus rejected it. Today, the code's own list. In its section on a Sikh's personal life, the Rehat Maryada names what a Sikh should not believe in.
In paraphrase: caste, untouchability, magic charms and spells, omens, auspicious days and times, horoscopes, and the worship of idols. Two very different things sit together there.
Caste and untouchability are about people: who counts as higher, who counts as unclean. Charms, omens and lucky days are about fear: trying to steer life with a thread or a calendar.
In Sikh teaching, both put something else where God should be. Caste first.
Guru Nanak, in a hymn in Raag Asa on Ang three hundred forty-nine, says in paraphrase: recognize the light in everyone, and don't ask about caste, because in the world beyond there is no caste.
If the same light is in every person, a ladder of birth is a fiction, and a cup that can't be shared is a lie about the person holding it.
That's why the langar is eaten side by side in rows, and why the prashad we met two days ago goes to everyone alike. Then the charms.
In Sikh teaching, what happens comes within God's hukam, the divine order.
A thread on the wrist can't bend it; a lucky Tuesday can't buy it. So a Sikh keeping the code doesn't wait for a lucky date to marry, travel or start a business; the day that works is the day.
Every person carries the same light, and every day belongs to the same Giver.

how: The Sikh Rehat Maryada asks Sikhs not to believe in caste, untouchability, charms, omens, auspicious days, horoscopes or idol worship, so Sikhs who keep the code don't choose dates for weddings and other ceremonies by the stars.

o: no ranking people by birth, since one light is in all
no marrying anyone from outside your own family group
no sharing meals with people of other faiths

games.q: inside the code's list: tap the pairs.
p: a ladder of birth among people
trying to steer life by fear

s: the code names some days as better for a wedding
it rejects auspicious days and times. the day that works is the day.
caste and charms sit in the same list in the code
both put something else where God should be.
Guru Nanak's hymn tells people to ask about caste first
it says recognize the light in everyone and don't ask about caste.

games.q: a Sikh couple is told their wedding date is unlucky and should move. what does the code say?
o: move it to a luckier month.
ask an astrologer to fix the stars.
no day is luckier; keep the date that works.
games.why: the code rejects auspicious days and horoscopes. in Sikh teaching every day falls within God's hukam.

practice: Look gently at your own small habits, a lucky shirt, knocking on wood, a number you avoid, and pick one, asking what it might be guarding against.
Then, just for this sit, set it down, and let the day ahead be a day, no luckier or unluckier than any other.

wordCard.voice: No caste. The Sikh code rejects caste and untouchability, and with them charms, omens, idols and lucky days, because the same light is in everyone. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi, as written in Gurbani: caste, birth group. Guru Nanak: don't ask about it.

carryVoice: Your line: no lucky days. The day that works is the day, whatever the calendar says. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sikh Rehat Maryada, a Sikh's personal life (living according to the Guru's tenets)
